mil5.1.7:0.4: 7. Question on the Disappearance of the True Teaching
mil5.1.7:1.1: “Venerable Nāgasena, this too was spoken by the Blessed One:
mil5.1.7:1.2: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:1.3: And again, at the time of his final Nibbāna, when the wanderer Subhadda asked a question, the Blessed One said:
mil5.1.7:1.4: ‘If these monks, Subhadda, were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of arahants.’ This statement is without remainder, without exception, and without qualification.
mil5.1.7:1.5: If, Venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata said,
mil5.1.7:1.6: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years,’ then the statement ‘the world would not be empty of arahants’ is false.
mil5.1.7:1.8: ‘the world would not be empty of arahants,’ then the statement ‘the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years’ is also false.
mil5.1.7:1.9: This is a two-horned dilemma. It is more tangled than the tangled, stronger than the strong, more knotted than the knotted. It has now come to you. Show here the power and range of your wisdom, like a sea-monster that has gone into the middle of the ocean.”
mil5.1.7:2.1: “This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One, your majesty: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:2.2: And at the time of his final Nibbāna, he said to the wanderer Subhadda:
mil5.1.7:2.3: ‘If these monks, Subhadda, were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of arahants.’
mil5.1.7:2.4: But those words of the Blessed One, your majesty, differ in meaning and differ in phrasing. The one is a limit placed on the Dispensation; the other is an exposition of practice. The two are far removed from each other.
mil5.1.7:2.5: Just as, your majesty, the sky is far removed from the earth, hell is far removed from heaven, the wholesome is far removed from the unwholesome, and pleasure is far removed from pain,
mil5.1.7:2.6: in the same way, your majesty, those two statements are far removed from each other.
mil5.1.7:3.1: “But, your majesty, so that your question may not be in vain, I will explain it in accordance with its essence. When the Blessed One said, ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years,’ he was pointing out its decline and setting a limit on what remained: ‘Ānanda, the true Dhamma would have lasted a thousand years if women had not gone forth.
mil5.1.7:3.2: Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:3.3: Now, your majesty, when the Blessed One spoke in this way, did he declare the disappearance of the true Dhamma, or did he reject the penetration (i.e. realisation of the Dhamma)?”
mil5.1.7:3.5: “He set a limit by declaring what remained, your majesty, while proclaiming what was lost.
mil5.1.7:3.6: Just as, your majesty, a man whose goods have been lost might take everything that remained and announce to the people, ‘This much of my property is lost; this is what is left.’
mil5.1.7:3.7: In the same way, your majesty, the Blessed One, proclaiming what was lost, told gods and humans what remained: ‘Now, Ānanda, the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years.’
mil5.1.7:3.8: So what the Blessed One said,
mil5.1.7:3.9: ‘the true Dhamma will last only five hundred years,’ is a statement of the limit of the Dispensation.
mil5.1.7:4.1: But when, at the time of his final Nibbāna, he spoke to the wanderer Subhadda, praising the ascetics, saying
mil5.1.7:4.2: ‘If these monks, Subhadda, were to live rightly, the world would not be empty of arahants,’ that is an exposition of practice. You, however, are treating the limit and the exposition as one and the same in essence.
